review.headline: Black Punishes Premature Flank Attacks in the London

sections.text: White opened aggressively on the kingside, but after 13.g4?? you struck back centrally with 13...fxe5! to rip open lines and win material. When White pushed again with 17.g5?, your queen entered the attack with 17...Qxg5!, leaving White's king stranded in the center.

You set up a pin on the d2-knight with 20...Rd3?! and soon broke through decisively. After White tried 22.f3, you executed 22...Qxf3+!, a sharp fork against the king on d1 and the rook on h1. That won the rook on h1 and left White completely dismantled.
White made a final error grabbing a pawn with 29.Qxb7?, allowing 29...Qxd2+! to win the knight. You traded queens into a completely winning endgame and efficiently mated with 62...Ra2#.

review.turning_point: White's overextended 13.g4?? allowed 13...fxe5!, giving you complete control over the center and launching your decisive attack.
review.focus: Look for dynamic queen entries instead of passive pawn moves, such as finding 18...Qg2 rather than 18...g6?!.

review.headline: An early gift squandered in a sharp Alekhine clash

sections.text: Your opponent gifted you an early piece with 3...Nxf2??, and you correctly recaptured with 4.Kxf2!. With an extra piece in hand, consolidating your lead was the main task.

Trouble began when you brought your queen out early. After Black attacked with 6...Nxe5, you played 7.Qh5??, pinning the f7-pawn against the king with 7.Qh5, but leaving your d3-bishop completely undefended. Black immediately punished this with 7...Nxd3+, wiping out your material advantage and seizing the initiative.
Your king was stranded in the center under heavy fire. Black pushed their central pawns and attacked your loose pieces, culminating in 23...Qxf3+ to seal the game.

review.turning_point: 7.Qh5?? was the decisive blunder, walking away from the defense of your bishop on d3 and handing the game over to Black after 7...Nxd3+.
review.focus: When ahead in material, prioritize simple development and piece coordination over premature queen attacks like 7.Qh5.

review.headline: A steady Philidor trade-down derailed by a wild pawn race

sections.text: You chose the Philidor Defense and aimed for a solid setup. After standard central trades, you missed a chance to grab a central pawn with 9...Nxe4, opting instead for 9...c6. Still, trading off queens and both pairs of rooks simplified the position cleanly into an equal same-color bishop endgame.

White blundered with 32.Kg3, letting your king invade with 32...Kd4+. You began sweeping up queenside pawns, but you took your eye off White's kingside threats. Grabbing on the queenside with 34...Kxb5 allowed White to eliminate your h-pawn via 35.Bxh7.

The endgame turned into a race. After 37.Bc2, marching your king away with 37...Kxa6 left White's f-pawn and h-pawn too fast. White offered you a lifeline with 38.f5, but 38...Be5 gave away control as White pushed forward to victory.

review.turning_point: Capturing 37...Kxa6 sent your king too far from the action, allowing White's kingside pawns to run away with the game.
review.focus: In pawn-race endgames, prioritize stopping your opponent's most dangerous passed pawns before collecting remote queenside material, as seen on 34...Kxb5 and 37...Kxa6.

review.headline: A rock-solid London System clash halted by an early truce

sections.text: You faced the Accelerated London System and set up with textbook solidity. By playing 2...e6 and contesting White's dark-squared bishop immediately with 3...Bd6, you signaled that you wouldn't let White control the diagonal without a fight. White retreated with 4.Bg3, and you calmly developed your pieces toward safety with 4...Nf6 and 5...O-O.

As White aligned the battery against your kingside with 6.Bd3 and 8.Qc2, you blunted the attack with 8...g6. You then developed your light-squared bishop via 7...b6 and 9...Bb7, putting long-range pressure across the board and securing a comfortable middlegame setup.

White tried to seize territory in the center with 10.Ne5, but you kept everything coordinated with 10...Qe7 and staked your own claim with 11...Ne4. Both sides had solid outposts and clean development when the game concluded in a peaceful draw.

review.turning_point: The position remained completely level after your active 11...Ne4, which contested the center and brought the game to an agreed draw.
review.focus: Try playing these equal positions further into the middlegame; after anchoring your knight with 11...Ne4, you had great prospects to fight for an advantage.

review.headline: A chaotic bullet skirmish full of hanging pieces

sections.text: The game exploded early when Black offered a bishop trade with 4...Be6. Rather than capturing, 5.d5 would have forked the bishop and knight. Instead, 5.dxe5 left your bishop on c4 hanging. Luckily, Black repeatedly missed capturing it, letting you fight back with 6.exd6.

The wild tactical misses continued in the center. After 8...d5, you found 9.exd5, hitting both the c6-knight and the e6-bishop. Black gave up the bishop on d5, and after 10.Re1 Qf6, 11.Bxd5 picked up the piece while establishing a strong pin on the d-file.

review.turning_point: Black's early error 4...Be6 handed you a massive chance, and despite traded inaccuracies, 11.Bxd5 consolidated a decisive four-pawn advantage before an abrupt resignation.
review.focus: Look for immediate pawn forks when opponent pieces line up on adjacent squares, such as playing 5.d5 instead of 5.dxe5.
